content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Wrongful restraint (old 339/341): voluntarily obstructing a person so as to prevent that person from proceeding in any direction in which they have a right to proceed. BNS restatement of IPC 339 / 341. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 126 is the rule on “Wrongful restraint”. The section provides that (1) Whoever voluntarily obstructs any person so as to prevent that person from proceeding in any direction in which that person has a right to proceed, is said wrongfully to restrain that person. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 126 exists so that “Wrongful restraint” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
126. (1) Whoever voluntarily obstructs any person so as to prevent that person from proceeding in any direction in which that person has a right to proceed, is said wrongfully to restrain that person

(2) Whoever wrongfully restrains any person shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both

Essential ingredients
1. (1) Whoever voluntarily obstructs any person so as to prevent that person from proceeding in any direction in which that person has a right to proceed, is said wrongfully to restrain that person
2. (2) Whoever wrongfully restrains any person shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). A obstructs a path along which Z has a right to pass, A not believing in good faith that he has a right to stop the path. Z is thereby prevented from passing. A wrongfully restrains Z

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 126 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Exceptions, limitations and provisos
Exception.—The obstruction of a private way over land or water which a person in good faith believes himself to have a lawful right to obstruct, is not an offence within the meaning of this section

hypotheticals.question: Whether BNS s. 126 (Wrongful restraint) applies, and how structured written arguments should be framed.
hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 126 (Wrongful restraint), Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) (1) Whoever voluntarily obstructs any person so as to prevent that person from proceeding in any direction in which that person has a right to proceed, is said wrongfully to restrain that person
   (2) (2) Whoever wrongfully restrains any person shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 126 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 126 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

Comprehensive Written Submissions. Deepen the doctrinal synthesis with four foundational layers.

Layer 1 — Place the section in the Chapter. Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.. Show why this heading sits where it sits.

Layer 2 — Work a second, slightly harder hypothetical. Change one ingredient and show why the section then fails.

Layer 3 — Distinction. Contrast BNS s. 126 with BNS s. 127. Write a short table in prose: meaning, ingredients, stage of the case, consequence. Confusion of neighbouring sections is the most common reason arguments collapse under judicial scrutiny.



Layer 5 — Application and current-law close. Apply the test to the problem facts in IRAC form (Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion). Close with: “The governing citation on or after 1 July 2024 is BNS s. 126.”

learningObjectives: Master the definition of wrongful restraint under BNS s. 126.
Analyze the single-direction obstruction requirement and the right of the person to proceed.
Examine the statutory Exception: good-faith obstruction of private ways.
Understand the punishment structure: imprisonment up to one month, fine up to ₹5,000, or both.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 126 defines wrongful restraint as voluntarily obstructing any person so as to prevent that person from proceeding in any direction in which that person has a right to proceed, punishable with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or both.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Protects individual freedom of physical movement by criminalizing unauthorized partial obstruction that prevents a person from travelling in a direction they have a legal right to go.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 126 (consolidating IPC ss. 339 and 341).
Sub-section (1): Definition — voluntarily obstructing any person so as to prevent proceeding in any direction in which they have a right to proceed.
Sub-section (2): Punishment — imprisonment up to one month, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both (fine modernized from ₹500 under IPC 341).
Exception: Obstruction of a private way over land or water which a person in good faith believes himself to have a lawful right to obstruct.
essentialIngredients: There was an obstruction preventing a person from proceeding.
The person obstructed had a legal right to proceed in that direction.
The obstruction prevented movement in a particular direction (partial restraint, not total confinement).
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 126 protects personal liberty in its simplest physical manifestation: the freedom to move in any direction one chooses. Wrongful restraint requires only a partial restriction: the victim is prevented from moving forward along a specific path or road, but remains completely free to stay where they are, turn around, or take another route. Physical contact is not necessary; locking a gate across a public highway, standing in a doorway with outstretched arms, or threatening violence if someone steps onto a public path constitutes wrongful restraint. The statutory Exception protects landowners or occupants who block a private path across their property under a bona fide, good-faith belief of legal right.
examples: Teaching example (Blocking a public highway): An accused parks his tractor across a narrow public village road and refuses to move it, preventing a doctor's car from proceeding to an emergency clinic. The doctor is free to turn back, but prevented from going forward. The accused is guilty of wrongful restraint under s. 126.

Teaching example (Good faith private pathway): A farmer fences off a dirt track running across his private agricultural field, genuinely believing under revenue records that the path is private and not a public easement. The farmer is protected by the statutory Exception.
distinctions: Wrongful Restraint (s. 126) vs Wrongful Confinement (s. 127): Wrongful restraint is partial obstruction in one direction (victim can move elsewhere); Wrongful confinement is total circumscribed restraint in all directions (victim cannot leave).
Wrongful Restraint vs Criminal Force (s. 129): Restraint can be achieved passively by physical barriers or words without using force; Criminal force requires causing motion or physical contact.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who stood in front of an office elevator and physically blocked a colleague from entering it, while leaving the stairs completely open, committed wrongful restraint.
Rule: Obstructing a person from proceeding in a direction in which they have a lawful right to proceed constitutes wrongful restraint under BNS s. 126.
Application: The colleague had a right to use the elevator; the accused voluntarily obstructed that direction of movement.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty under BNS s. 126.

keyTakeaways: Consolidates IPC ss. 339 and 341 into a unified section.
Partial obstruction preventing movement in a specific direction.
The victim must have a legal right to proceed in that direction.
Punishable with up to one month imprisonment, fine up to ₹5,000, or both.
